claim: The murine cerebellum has a simple alignment of 8-10 stereotypical folds along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: The murine cerebellum has a simple alignment of 8–10 stereotypical folds along the anterior-posterior axis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the anatomical structure of the murine cerebellum, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The developing cerebellum has a temporary external granule cell layer (EGL) of proliferating granule cell precursors that cover the surface.
source: The developing cerebellum is distinct from the cerebral cortex, as it has a temporary external granule cell layer (EGL) of proliferating granule cell precursors that cover the surface and generate growth primarily in the anterior-posterior (AP) direction (Leto et al., 2016; Legué et al., 2015; Legué et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Leto et al., 2016; Legué et al., 2015; Legué et al., 2016).

claim: The EGL generates growth primarily in the anterior-posterior direction.
source: The developing cerebellum is distinct from the cerebral cortex, as it has a temporary external granule cell layer (EGL) of proliferating granule cell precursors that cover the surface and generate growth primarily in the anterior-posterior (AP) direction (Leto et al., 2016; Legué et al., 2015; Legué et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During development a thickening occurs in the EGL at the base of each forming fissure, termed anchoring center (AC).
source: During development a thickening occurs in the EGL at the base of each forming fissure, termed anchoring center (AC) (Sudarov and Joyner, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Sudarov and Joyner, 2007).

claim: In the adult cerebellum the inner granule cell layer (IGL) is thinnest at the ACs.
source: whereas in the adult cerebellum the inner granule cell layer (IGL), generated by the EGL during the first two weeks of life, is thinnest at the ACs.
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical structure of the adult cerebellum, based on established knowledge.

claim: Neither the molecular layer nor the IGL are present when folding is initiated in the embryo.
source: However, neither the molecular layer nor the IGL are present when folding is initiated in the embryo.
evidence: This is a statement about the developmental timing of cerebellar structures, based on established knowledge.

claim: A bilayer system consisting of the EGL and underlying core is a more appropriate approximation for cerebellar folding than a tri-layer elastic model.
source: Therefore we argue that a bilayer system consisting of the EGL and underlying core, is a more appropriate approximation for cerebellar folding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the molecular layer and IGL are not present at folding initiation.

claim: Cerebellar folding emerges from differential expansion between an un-patterned, rapidly expanding EGL and an underlying core.
source: Here we show that cerebellar folding emerges from differential expansion between an un-patterned, rapidly expanding EGL and an underlying core.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The measured stiffness differential, compressive forces, and the thickness variation in the EGL are all inconsistent with traditional elastic wrinkling models driven by differential growth.
source: Additionally, we demonstrate that the measured stiffness differential, compressive forces, and the thickness variation in the EGL are all inconsistent with traditional elastic wrinkling models driven by differential growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The expansion of the EGL is uniform and fluid-like.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the expansion of the EGL is uniform, and fluid-like
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cerebellum is under radial and circumferential constraints when folding initiates.
source: and that the cerebellum is under radial and circumferential constraints when folding initiates.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A multi-phase model incorporating differential expansion of a fluid outer layer and radial and circumferential constraints approximates the in vivo shape evolution observed during initiation of cerebellar folding.
source: Lastly, we find that a multi-phase model incorporating differential expansion of a fluid outer layer and radial and circumferential constraints approximates the in vivo shape evolution observed during initiation of cerebellar folding.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by modeling constrained by experimental data.

claim: At E16.5 and E17.5 the ratios of growth between the EGL and core closely approximated the expansion of a semi-circle.
source: Of significance, we found that at E16.5 and E17.5 the ratios of growth between the EGL and core closely approximated the expansion of a semi-circle.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1f.

claim: At E18.5 and P0 the expansion rate of the EGL was greater than the rate of core expansion.
source: However, at E18.5 and P0 the expansion rate of the EGL was greater than the rate of core expansion (Figure 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The cerebellum remains unfolded during the initial proportional expansion between the EGL and core.
source: Indeed, we found that the cerebellum remains unfolded during the initial proportional expansion between the EGL and core and only folds when the differential expansion is initiated (Figure 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by folding index measurements shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The cerebellum only folds when the differential expansion is initiated.
source: Indeed, we found that the cerebellum remains unfolded during the initial proportional expansion between the EGL and core and only folds when the differential expansion is initiated (Figure 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by folding index measurements shown in Figure 1g.

claim: To produce the observed number of folds at initiation of folding through wrinkling based models constrained by measurements of the embryonic cerebellum, a large stiffness ratio of around 50 was required.
source: We found that to produce the observed number of folds (three in the semi-circular cerebellum and six in the circular model) at initiation of folding through wrinkling based models constrained by our measurements of the embryonic cerebellum, a large stiffness ratio was required of around 50.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The EGL has a slightly higher instantaneous bulk modulus than the core at all stages measured from E16.5 to P18.5.
source: Using this estimation, we found that the EGL has a slightly higher instantaneous bulk modulus than the core at all stages measured.
evidence: This claim is supported by scanning acoustic microscopy measurements shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: The ratio of bulk modulus between EGL and core was approximately 1.05:1.
source: Unsurprisingly, the ratio (~1.05:1) was not close to being sufficient to produce a folding wavelength similar to that in the cerebellum (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by scanning acoustic microscopy measurements shown in Figure 2b-d.

claim: The stiffness ratio of 1.05:1 was not sufficient to produce a folding wavelength similar to that in the cerebellum.
source: Unsurprisingly, the ratio (~1.05:1) was not close to being sufficient to produce a folding wavelength similar to that in the cerebellum (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of modeling predictions with experimental measurements.

claim: Radial cuts through the EGL and into the core of live E16.5 tissue slices result in the EGL opening.
source: Time-lapse imaging revealed that, in contrast to the prediction, the EGL opens as well as part of the underlying cut in the core (Figure 2f–h, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–c, and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2f-h and Video 1.

claim: The opening of the EGL after cutting indicates there is circumferential tension within the outer layers of the cerebellum.
source: This result indicates there is circumferential tension within the outer layers of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the EGL opens after cutting.

claim: At E16.5-18.5, the EGL was found to be 1.2-1.4 times thicker in the ACs than in the surrounding EGL.
source: Not all cerebella have visible AC at E16.5. However in the subset that do and in the three ACs present at E17.5, the EGL was found to be 1.2–1.4 times thicker in the ACs than in the surrounding EGL (Figure 2i–l and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by thickness measurements shown in Figure 2i-l.

claim: The thickness ratio of EGL in ACs compared to surrounding EGL increased to 1.7 times at E18.5.
source: Moreover, the thickness ratio increased to 1.7 times at E18.5 (Figure 2l).
evidence: This claim is supported by thickness measurements shown in Figure 2l.

claim: The proliferation rates were similar in the three regions (L123, L45, L678) at E16.5.
source: Interestingly, we found that the proliferation rates were similar in the three regions at E16.5 (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation measurements shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The EGL proliferation rate at E17.5 in L678 was slightly reduced compared to the L123 region.
source: The EGL proliferation rate at E17.5 in L678 was slightly reduced compared to the L123 region, but no other differences were found (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation measurements shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Proliferation is uniform just before initiation of folding.
source: Thus proliferation is uniform just before initiation of folding and the small difference found during folding does not correlate with lobule size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proliferation measurements at E16.5 and E17.5.

claim: Lobule size is not determined by modulating the levels of proliferation at the onset of folding.
source: This result indicates that lobule size is not determined by modulating the levels of proliferation at the onset of folding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that proliferation rates are uniform at folding initiation.

claim: The rate of proliferation within each forming AC region at E16.5 and E17.5 was the same as in the surrounding EGL.
source: We found the rate of proliferation within each forming AC region at E16.5 and E17.5 was the same as in the surrounding EGL (Figure 3e,f)
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation measurements shown in Figure 3e,f.

claim: Proliferation within all regions of the EGL at the initiation of folding is uniform.
source: thus proliferation within all regions of the EGL at the initiation of folding is uniform.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proliferation measurements in different regions and ACs.

claim: Regional modulation of proliferation does not form or position the ACs.
source: Furthermore, regional modulation of proliferation does not form or position the ACs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that proliferation is uniform in ACs and surrounding regions.

claim: At E18.5, the rate of proliferation was significantly lower in the L678 region compared with the L123 and L45 regions.
source: At E18.5, after the initiation of folding, we found that the rate of proliferation was significantly lower in the L678 region compared with the L123 and L45 regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Proliferation within the ACs at E18.5 remained uniform with the surrounding regions.
source: However, proliferation within the ACs at E18.5 remained uniform with the surrounding regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: There was no difference in cell shape in the different lobule regions of the EGL or between the AC areas and the surrounding EGL at E16.5 and E18.5.
source: However, we found no difference in cell shape in the different lobule regions of the EGL or between the AC areas and the surrounding EGL at each age (Figure 3h,i).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell shape measurements shown in Figure 3h,i.

claim: Cell size was uniform at E16.5 and E18.5 except for a slight reduction in L678 at E16.5 when compared with L123 and the AC regions.
source: Cell size was uniform at both stages except for a slight reduction in L678 at E16.5 when compared with L123 and the AC regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell size measurements shown in Figure 3j,k.

claim: The size of cells is reduced at E18.5 compared to E16.5.
source: However, the size of cells is reduced at E18.5 compared to E16.5 (Figure 3j,k and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell size measurements shown in Figure 3j,k and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The proliferating GCPs that drive expansion of the EGL have both uniform proliferation rates and similar shapes and sizes across the lobule regions defined by the first three ACs at folding initiation.
source: Thus, the proliferating GCPs that drive expansion of the EGL have both uniform proliferation rates and similar shapes and sizes across the lobule regions defined by the first three ACs at folding initiation.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the proliferation, cell shape, and cell size measurements.

claim: The Bergmann glial and radial glial fibers are distributed evenly along the AP axis of the EGL.
source: This analysis showed that the Bergmann glial and radial glial fibers are distributed evenly along the AP axis of the EGL, and therefore are not directing the positions where folding initiates based on an uneven regional distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber density measurements shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Bergmann glial and radial glial fibers are not directing the positions where folding initiates based on an uneven regional distribution.
source: This analysis showed that the Bergmann glial and radial glial fibers are distributed evenly along the AP axis of the EGL, and therefore are not directing the positions where folding initiates based on an uneven regional distribution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fiber distribution is uniform.

claim: Cuts made in live E16.5 tissue slices between the EGL and VZ reveal tension directed radially within the cerebellum.
source: As predicted, after cutting the tissue relaxed revealing tension directed radially within the cerebellum (Figure 4d,e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue cutting experiments shown in Figure 4c-e and Video 2.

claim: Only the horizontal cuts opened along the full length of the cut although they opened more slowly than radial cuts.
source: Interestingly, quantification of how the radial and horizontal cuts open revealed that only the horizontal cuts opened along the full length of the cut although they opened more slowly than radial cuts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2g–j)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of tissue cutting experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2g-j.

claim: At the time of folding initiation the EGL is growing uniformly.
source: Taken together, at the time of folding initiation the EGL, which is driving the differential expansion, is itself growing uniformly and the cerebellum is under both radial and circumferential constraints.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the proliferation and tissue cutting experiments.

claim: At the time of folding initiation the cerebellum is under both radial and circumferential constraints.
source: Taken together, at the time of folding initiation the EGL, which is driving the differential expansion, is itself growing uniformly and the cerebellum is under both radial and circumferential constraints.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the tissue cutting experiments.

claim: There is no evidence of any pre-patterning in the EGL in either cellular behaviors or fiber distribution.
source: Finally, there is no evidence of any pre-patterning in the EGL in either cellular behaviors or fiber distribution.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the proliferation, cell shape, cell size, and fiber distribution measurements.

claim: Granule cells within the EGL are highly motile within the EGL.
source: Tracking the cell positions through time revealed that granule cells within the EGL are highly motile within the EGL.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5 and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: There was no obvious directionality or collectivity to the movement of granule cells within the EGL.
source: Furthermore, there was no obvious directionality or collectivity to the movement.
evidence: This is an observation from the live imaging data shown in Figure 5 and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: The dynamic motility of granule cells results in the constant exchanging of nearest neighbors over the course of tens to hundreds of minutes.
source: However, the dynamic motility resulted in the constant exchanging of nearest neighbors over the course of tens to hundreds of minutes and shows that at the timescale of folding the EGL is more fluid-like than a solid epithelial layer (Figure 5 and Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5 and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: At the timescale of folding the EGL is more fluid-like than a solid epithelial layer.
source: However, the dynamic motility resulted in the constant exchanging of nearest neighbors over the course of tens to hundreds of minutes and shows that at the timescale of folding the EGL is more fluid-like than a solid epithelial layer (Figure 5 and Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of dynamic cell rearrangement in the EGL.

claim: The multi-phase model closely approximates the phase and amplitude behavior of EGL thickness and radius oscillations from E16.5 through E18.5.
source: Solving the analytical model as constrained by our measured embryonic data we found that it closely approximates the phase and amplitude behavior of EGL thickness and radius oscillations from E16.5 through E18.5. (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6a-c.

claim: The multi-phase model is not able to produce self-contacting folds or hierarchical folding.
source: However, the model is not able to produce self-contacting folds or hierarchical folding, both of which are seen in the cerebellum at later stages.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model identified by the authors.

claim: In the lobule regions that undergo folding there is a temporal correlation between when the onset of sub-folding and differential expansion occur.
source: We found that indeed in the lobule regions that undergo folding there is a temporal correlation between when the onset of sub-folding and differential expansion occur (Figure 7a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 7a-d.

claim: The L45 region that does not fold during the same time period has a different, more rectangular shape.
source: In contrast, the region (L45) that does not fold during the same time period has a different, more rectangular shape, and the ratio of EGL growth to core growth is proportional for a rectangle during the time measured (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 7.

claim: The ratio of EGL growth to core growth in L45 is proportional for a rectangle during the time measured.
source: In contrast, the region (L45) that does not fold during the same time period has a different, more rectangular shape, and the ratio of EGL growth to core growth is proportional for a rectangle during the time measured (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 7.

claim: Traditional morphometric cellular behaviors such as changes in cell shape, size and proliferation do not direct where cerebellar folding initiates.
source: Thus, traditional morphometric cellular behaviors such as changes in cell shape, size and proliferation do not direct where cerebellar folding initiates.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings showing uniform proliferation, cell shape, and cell size.

claim: Adjusting the amount of tension spanning the cerebellum will change the degree of folding.
source: One such prediction is that adjusting the amount of tension spanning the cerebellum will change the degree of folding.
evidence: This is a prediction from the multi-phase model.

claim: Alterations of the cells that likely create tension-based forces could explain the dramatically disrupted folding seen in mouse mutants in which radial glia do not produce Bergmann glia.
source: Indeed, alterations of the cells that likely create tension-based forces could explain the dramatically disrupted folding seen in mouse mutants in which radial glia do not produce Bergmann glia (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model predictions and observations from mutant mice cited in Li et al., 2014.

claim: Without Bergmann glia, the EGL would be expected to not form a layer with regular thickness and it should be more sensitive to variations in radial glial tension.
source: Without Bergmann glia, the EGL would be expected to not form a layer with regular thickness and it should be more sensitive to variations in radial glial tension.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the role of Bergmann glia in the model.

claim: Mutants without Bergmann glia have more localized and less regular folds.
source: Consistent with this prediction, mutants without Bergmann glia have more localized and less regular folds (Li et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research (Li et al., 2014).

claim: To approximate the observed shape changes in the murine cerebellum from E17.5 to E18.5 the ratio of the core stiffness over the radial tension must increase.
source: Under the new framework revealed by our measurements made in the developing mouse cerebellum, to approximate the observed shape changes in the murine cerebellum from E17.5 to E18.5 the ratio of the core stiffness over the radial tension must increase.
evidence: This is a prediction from the multi-phase model.

claim: The measured bulk modulus of the core shows no increase during development.
source: Yet, the measured bulk modulus of the core shows no increase during development.
evidence: This is based on the scanning acoustic microscopy measurements.

claim: Radial tension must decrease during development.
source: Therefore a second prediction is that radial tension must decrease during development.
evidence: This is a prediction from the multi-phase model based on the observation that core stiffness does not increase.

claim: Radial glial fibers are an attractive candidate to mediate the change in radial tension.
source: While the cerebellum is crossed by many fibers at folding initiation, radial glial fibers are an attractive candidate to mediate this change in radial tension (Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Rahimi-Balaei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Radial glia span from the VZ to the surface of the cerebellum at E16.5.
source: First, they span from the VZ to the surface of the cerebellum at E16.5.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about radial glia.

claim: During folding initiation the radial glia undergo a transition into Bergmann glia where they release their basal connection to the VZ and the cell body migrates towards the surface.
source: Additionally, during folding initiation the radial glia undergo a transition into Bergmann glia where they release their basal connection to the VZ and the cell body migrates towards the surface (Mota and Herculano-Houzel, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The transition of radial glia into Bergmann glia could lead to a reduction in the global radial tension.
source: This transition could lead to a reduction in the global radial tension and thus would be consistent with our model prediction.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the biological process and model predictions.

claim: ACs maintain their spatial positions.
source: As ACs maintain their spatial positions, and as they compartmentalize granule cells within the EGL into the lobule regions (Legué et al., 2015), we propose that they create fixed mechanical boundaries that divide the cerebellum into self-similar domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: ACs compartmentalize granule cells within the EGL into the lobule regions.
source: As ACs maintain their spatial positions, and as they compartmentalize granule cells within the EGL into the lobule regions (Legué et al., 2015), we propose that they create fixed mechanical boundaries that divide the cerebellum into self-similar domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: ACs create fixed mechanical boundaries that divide the cerebellum into self-similar domains.
source: As ACs maintain their spatial positions, and as they compartmentalize granule cells within the EGL into the lobule regions (Legué et al., 2015), we propose that they create fixed mechanical boundaries that divide the cerebellum into self-similar domains.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the properties of ACs.

claim: Once separated by ACs, the lobule regions can develop distinct characteristics, like the observed differential proliferation rates at E18.5.
source: Furthermore since ACs compartmentalize granule cells within the lobule regions, once separated the lobule regions can develop distinct characteristics, like the observed differential proliferation rates at E18.5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the compartmentalization by ACs and the observed differential proliferation.

claim: The folding patterns seen across cerebella in different species evolved by adjustment of global as well as regional levels of differential expansion and tension.
source: We speculate, therefore, that the folding patterns seen across cerebella in different species evolved by adjustment of global as well as regional levels of differential expansion and tension which ultimately mold the functionality of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a speculation about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: Radial glia span the entire cerebral cortex just as in the cerebellum.
source: Radial glia span the entire cerebral cortex just as in the cerebellum (Götz et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Species with folded cerebrums have evolved outer radial glial cells for which the cell body leaves the ventricular zone to become positioned near the surface while retaining fibers anchored on the surface, similar to Bergmann glia in the cerebellum.
source: Furthermore, species with folded cerebrums have evolved outer radial glial cells for which the cell body leaves the ventricular zone to become positioned near the surface while retaining fibers anchored on the surface, similar to Bergmann glia in the cerebellum (Leung and Li, 2018; Reillo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tissue cutting in the cerebral cortex of ferrets has revealed a similar tension pattern during folding as found in the cerebellum.
source: Tissue cutting in the cerebral cortex of ferrets has revealed a similar tension pattern during folding as we found in the cerebellum (Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Outer radial glial cells proliferate to drive the expansion of the outer regions of the cerebral cortex around the time of initiation of folding.
source: However, outer radial glial cells proliferate, much like the GCPs of the EGL, to drive the expansion of the outer regions of the cerebral cortex around the time of initiation of folding (Hansen et al., 2010; Heng et al., 2017; Nowakowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The cerebellum houses 80% of the neurons in the human brain.
source: The cerebellum, housing 80% of the neurons in the human brain may be an extreme example requiring the region of proliferation to be completely on the outer surface (Andersen et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The unfolded murine cerebellum is a simple cylinder-like structure elongated in the medio-lateral axis.
source: Unlike the cerebral cortex, the unfolded murine cerebellum is a simple cylinder-like structure elongated in the medio-lateral axis (Figure 1e) (Szulc et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1e.

claim: All folds in the medial cerebellum (vermis) are aligned in the same axis.
source: All folds in the medial cerebellum (vermis) are aligned in the same axis allowing 2-D measurements to estimate expansion in the anterior-posterior axis of the vermis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: In cross-section the unfolded cerebellum approximates a semicircle.
source: In cross-section the unfolded cerebellum approximates a semicircle
evidence: This is based on observation of cerebellar anatomy.

claim: Small modulus contrasts have been reported for other brain regions with multiple loading modes.
source: Consistent with our finding, small modulus contrasts have been reported for other brain regions with multiple loading modes, such as shear, compression, and tension (Xu et al., 2010; Lejeune et al., 2016; Budday et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Elastic material models with graded growth profiles predict folding of cerebral cortex without a large stiffness differential.
source: Elastic material models with graded growth profiles have been developed that predict folding of cerebral cortex without a large stiffness differential (Tallinen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Elastic simulations predict the EGL remains closed after cutting.
source: Elastic bi-layer wrinkling models predict compressive forces in the outer layer. Simulations performed of cuts through the outer layer and into the inner layer predict that upon relaxation the outer layer should not open (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a prediction from elastic bilayer simulations shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The elastic bi-layer model requires the EGL to be thinnest at the base of each AC.
source: The elastic bi-layer model requires the EGL to be thinnest at the base of each AC, which are the lowest parts of the cerebellar surface. Thus, the EGL should have an 'in-phase' thickness variation.
evidence: This is a requirement of elastic bilayer models based on mechanical equilibrium.

claim: Without in-phase thickness variation, a purely elastic model cannot be in mechanical equilibrium in the quasistatic limit.
source: Without this feature, a purely elastic model – bi-layer based or even graded growth profile based – cannot be in mechanical equilibrium (in the quasistatic limit) (Engstrom et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The embryonic EGL is thickest in the ACs when folding initiates.
source: However, we previously reported that the embryonic EGL is thickest in the ACs when folding initiates, that is it has an 'out-of-phase' thickness variation (Sudarov and Joyner, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The final thickness variations of the IGL and molecular layer of the cerebellar cortex are in-phase.
source: As described above, the final thickness variations of the IGL (as well as the molecular layer) of the cerebellar cortex are in-phase, just as the layers of the adult cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about adult cerebellar anatomy.

claim: The EGL drives the majority of cerebellar growth.
source: Since the EGL drives the majority of cerebellar growth (Leto et al., 2016; Legué et al., 2015; Legué et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the multi-phase model, EGL thickness oscillations are found to be out-of-phase with the surface height (radius) oscillations when 0 < μ/kr <1.
source: In contrast with the elastic bilayer wrinkling model, EGL thickness oscillations are found to be out-of-phase with the surface height (radius) oscillations when 0 < μ/kr <1.
evidence: This is a prediction from the multi-phase model.

claim: In the multi-phase model, the number of initial folds does not depend on the thickness of the EGL, but only on material properties.
source: Note that in contrast with elastic wrinkling, the number of initial folds does not depend on the thickness (a length scale) of the EGL, but only on material properties.
evidence: This is a prediction from the multi-phase model that contrasts with elastic wrinkling models.

claim: The multi-phase model assumes circumferential tension in addition to radial tension.
source: Given that our tissue cutting and relaxation experiment revealed circumferential tension in the cerebellum at folding initiation (Figure 2f–h, Video 1), we returned to the mathematics and found a previously unrealized geometric relationship in the circular limit of the model that in fact assumes circumferential tension in addition to the previously discussed radial tension given that the perimeter of a circle is determined by its radius.
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical formulation of the model.
